Judgement, as one of the core tenets of medicine, relies upon the integration of multilayered data with nuanced decision making. Cancer offers a unique context for medical decisions given not only its variegated forms with evolution of disease but also the need to take into account the individual condition of patients, their ability to receive treatment, and their responses to treatment. Challenges remain in the accurate detection, characterization, and monitoring of cancers despite improved technologies. Radiographic assessment of disease most commonly relies upon visual evaluations, the interpretations of which may be augmented by advanced computational analyses. In particular, artificial intelligence (AI) promises to make great strides in the qualitative interpretation of cancer imaging by expert clinicians, including volumetric delineation of tumors over time, extrapolation of the tumor genotype and biological course from its radiographic phenotype, prediction of clinical outcome, and assessment of the impact of disease and treatment on adjacent organs. AI may automate processes in the initial interpretation of images and shift the clinical workflow of radiographic detection, management decisions on whether or not to administer an intervention, and subsequent observation to a yet to be envisioned paradigm. Here, the authors review the current state of AI as applied to medical imaging of cancer and describe advances in 4 tumor types (lung, brain, breast, and prostate) to illustrate how common clinical problems are being addressed. Upon successful prospective validation, this AI algorithm could hold enormous potential to identify individuals at high risk for future events in organised or opportunistic screening settings at low additional costs and high speed. However, implementation of such algorithms could also lead to an information overflow without tangible clinical benefits. Thus, rigorous validation and demonstration of actual clinical consequences are required before these methods can be introduced into clinical practice. Here, we describe the potential of AI algorithms as used by Pickhardt and colleagues with implications for the broader field, and we identify obstacles that could hamper clinical introduction. So far, huge amounts of imaging data are acquired every day, but only a small proportion of the information contained in the scans is used to confirm or rule out a medical condition. The vast majority of information in the image is not quantified because reliable and efficient ways for extraction are missing. The authors' study presents an interesting example of how recent advances in automated AI techniques, both engineered and deep learning based, have introduced the possibility for high-throughput quantification of imaging biomarkers in an automated manner. This is not only due to the time-consuming nature of quantification but, more importantly, also due to the unknown risks and benefits of clinical implementation. Pickhardt and colleagues' automated AI algorithms address the former; however, the latter remains largely unknown. Therefore, a proof of clinical value is mandated to comprehensively assess the risks versus benefits of such a new system. This proof should include the demonstration of reclassification of risk into different risk categories with therapeutic implications, accounting for concomitant medical therapy and other information available at the time of imaging (such as other diagnostic tests). Other factors that need to be considered are the additional costs of the AI, even though they might be low, as well as false negative or positive findings. From an imaging standpoint, thorough investigation and description of biases and variance are crucial to ensure clinical validity and robustness. This investigation includes the definition of acquisition and reconstruction protocols to account for differences between vendors and institutions. In addition, the expertise and understanding of the end user regarding the use and output of biomarkers need to be explored to provide recommendations for correct application. Consequently, each biomarker should be accompanied by detailed user guidelines, in which requirements and limitations for reliable and safe implementation are described. Although several obstacles—from a development as well as clinical implementation perspective—need to be addressed before widespread use of AI imaging biomarkers is possible, their implementation could represent a fundamental change in the way radiology data are interpreted and used. Leveraging the power of AI techniques for large-scale screening has the possibility to accelerate improvement of population health in several facets of health care.
